_doc: Facts that describe a problem. The extractor emits facts from this vocabulary only; rules.dl and learned.dl turn them into a schema plus parameters. Every fact implicitly starts with the problem id, which the driver adds. 'values' lists the allowed constants; the placeholder <int> stands for any integer written as a string (e.g. "-1") and <char> for any single character. 'param' means one of the function's parameter names.

arg.doc: type of each parameter (a grid parameter needs no separate grid fact). interval_list = list of [start, end] integer pairs; the end-point convention (closed or half-open) is set with interval_ends. int_matrix = list of rows of integers (used with ask diagonal_sums or matrix_transform; give iterate on it). op_list = list of operation tuples ('push', x) with integer x, ('pop',) and optionally ('peek',) (used with ask simulate_ops; give iterate on it)

iterate.doc: the answer is computed from the elements of this list (or the characters of this string)

keep.doc: only elements satisfying cond take part; several keep facts mean all must hold. vowel = a/e/i/o/u any case; consonant = ASCII letter that is not a vowel. letter = any Unicode letter (str.isalpha, includes é, ï); ascii_letter = a-z or A-Z only; consonant = ASCII letter that is not a vowel

remainder.doc: only integer elements x with x % m == r (Python's %, so for positive m the remainder is in 0..m-1 and negative numbers get a non-negative remainder, e.g. -1 % 4 == 3) take part; m must be non-zero. Use r = 0 for 'divisible by m' / 'multiple of m': ["remainder", "5", "0"]. Zero and negative multiples then count too, so add keep positive / drop zero when the statement excludes them. Combines with keep/drop (all must hold); several remainder facts must all hold. Applied to the original element, before map, floordiv, scale and add. Only tests equality

bound.doc: only integer elements x compared with the constant n take part: ge = x >= n, gt = x > n, le = x <= n, lt = x < n. The abs_ ops compare the MAGNITUDE |x| instead: abs_ge = |x| >= n, abs_gt = |x| > n, abs_le = |x| <= n, abs_lt = |x| < n (e.g. 'absolute value strictly less than 50' is ["bound","abs_lt","50"]). Use two facts for a range, e.g. 1 <= v <= 100 is ["bound","ge","1"] plus ["bound","le","100"]; an annulus 10 <= |x| < 50 is abs_ge 10 plus abs_lt 50. Applied to the original element (before map, floordiv, scale and add, so it is independent of map abs); combines with keep/drop/remainder (all must hold); several allowed

digit_sum_test.doc: only integer elements whose decimal digit sum s (computed on the absolute value, so -13 has digit sum 4 and 0 has digit sum 0) satisfy s % m == r take part; m must be non-zero. 'digit sum is even' is ["digit_sum_test","2","0"], 'digit sum is odd' is ["digit_sum_test","2","1"], 'digit sum divisible by 3' is ["digit_sum_test","3","0"]. Applied to the original element, before map, floordiv, scale and add; combines with keep/drop/remainder/bound/digit_sum_bound (all must hold); several allowed. seq_fold over integers only

digit_sum_bound.doc: only integer elements whose decimal digit sum s (of the absolute value) compares true with the constant n take part: ge = s >= n, gt = s > n, le = s <= n, lt = s < n, eq = s == n, ne = s != n. E.g. 'digit sum at least 10' is ["digit_sum_bound","ge","10"]. Applied to the original element, before map, floordiv, scale and add; combines with all other element filters (all must hold); several allowed. seq_fold over integers only

map.doc: applied to each kept element before aggregation (at most one)

floordiv.doc: each kept integer element is floor-divided by the non-zero integer constant n using Python's // (rounds toward negative infinity, so -7 // 2 == -4; exact for multiples of n). Applied after the optional map fn and BEFORE scale and add. With add it expresses x // n + b: 'entry // 6 + 1' is ["floordiv", "6"] plus ["add", "1"]. At most one; integer elements only; seq_fold, select_rank, fold and palindrome_check only

scale.doc: each kept element is multiplied by the integer constant n (n may be negative or zero), applied after the optional map fn and floordiv and BEFORE add. With add it expresses a*x + b: 3 * entry - 4 is ["scale", "3"] plus ["add", "-4"]; for '(x + b) * n' fold the constant yourself (n*x + n*b). At most one; integer elements only

add.doc: integer constant n added to each kept element after the optional map fn, floordiv and scale, before aggregation (use a negative n for subtraction). Example: ["add", "10"] gives x + 10. At most one; integer elements only

distinct.doc: deduplicate for a seq_fold (any aggregate), a select_rank or a fold. original: repeated ORIGINAL elements count once (first occurrence kept, order preserved) before filtering/map/floordiv/scale/add, so -9 and 9 stay different even with map abs. mapped: duplicates are removed from the final mapped values just before aggregation/selection, so -9 and 9 under map abs collapse to one. At most one. Example: ["distinct", "original"] with remainder 9 0, drop zero, map abs, aggregate sum = sum of |v| over distinct nonzero multiples of 9

aggregate.doc: how kept (mapped) elements become the answer; list keeps order, join concatenates strings; distinct_count counts distinct kept (mapped) values. Do NOT combine with select_rank (use select_rank instead of aggregate for k-th largest/smallest) nor with fold (use fold for gcd/lcm/bitwise reductions) is_palindrome (bool) tells whether the kept (mapped) sequence reads the same reversed (e.g. chars source + keep alnum + map lower).

fold.doc: the answer is the integer reduction of the kept, mapped elements of the iterated int list: gcd = greatest common divisor (non-negative; a single element gives its absolute value; zeros are neutral), lcm = least common multiple (non-negative; any zero element makes it 0), bit_and / bit_or / bit_xor = bitwise AND / OR / XOR of all of them. Use INSTEAD of aggregate. The same keep/drop/remainder/bound/map/floordiv/scale/add/distinct filters apply (digit_sum filters are not supported). if_empty is REQUIRED: it is the answer when no element remains (e.g. gcd of an empty list is 0 in many statements: ["if_empty","0"]; lcm is often 1; use none for None). Example 'greatest common divisor of all numbers, 0 for an empty list': ["arg","nums","int_list"], ["iterate","nums"], ["fold","gcd"], ["if_empty","0"]. Example 'gcd of the even numbers': add ["keep","even"]. Example 'XOR of all values': ["fold","bit_xor"]

select_rank.doc: the answer is the k-th largest or k-th smallest (k = 1 is the maximum / minimum) of the kept, mapped elements of the iterated list (the same keep/drop/remainder/bound/map/floordiv/scale/add filters apply; digit_sum filters are not supported); use INSTEAD of aggregate. Duplicates count separately unless ["distinct", scope] is given, so 'second largest distinct value' needs ["distinct","mapped"] (or original) and 'second largest including repeats' does not. k is an integer constant or the name of an int parameter (declared with arg int). if_empty is REQUIRED: it is the answer when fewer than k elements remain (or k < 1), e.g. ["if_empty","none"]. Example 'second largest distinct value, None if fewer than two': ["arg","scores","int_list"], ["iterate","scores"], ["select_rank","largest","2"], ["distinct","mapped"], ["if_empty","none"]. Example 'k-th smallest of the even numbers': ["select_rank","smallest","k"], ["keep","even"], ["arg","k","int"], ["if_empty","-1"]

if_empty.doc: answer when no element is kept (required for max/min) or, with select_rank or fold, when fewer than k elements remain / no element remains (required). With ask simulate_ops it is the value a pop or peek on an empty container yields (optional, default none). With ask best_pair it is the answer when the list has fewer than two elements (required)

passable.doc: grid cells holding this character belong to regions / can be walked on; give one fact per character

ask.doc: the question being asked. Grid asks (arg grid + passable): count_components (0 for an empty grid), largest_component (0 when no cell is passable), shortest_path. Knapsack asks (items + target): min_count, count_ways, feasible. Interval asks (arg interval_list, also give iterate on it): max_overlap = the maximum number of intervals open at any single time (minimum rooms/resources so that no overlapping intervals share one), 0 for an empty list, add ["at_least", n] to get the boolean 'maximum overlap >= n' instead; merge_intervals = merge intervals sharing at least one point and answer the merged [start, end] lists sorted by start ([] for an empty list, input not modified), add ["interval_output", form] to answer a number derived from the merged intervals instead; overlap_pairs = count unordered pairs of different valid (non-empty) intervals (different list positions, identical entries form a pair) that share a point (default), or with ["pair_relation","disjoint"] that do not; ["pair_output","exists"|"all"] gives a boolean instead of the count; 0 for an empty list; covered_length = the number of integer points (closed ends) or total length (half-open ends) whose coverage depth, i.e. the number of valid intervals containing the point counting multiplicity, lies within [min_depth, max_depth] (min_depth default 1, max_depth default unbounded); 0 for an empty list. Example 'integers covered by at least two spans': ["ask","covered_length"], ["min_depth","2"], ["interval_ends","closed"]; 'covered by exactly two' adds ["max_depth","2"]. All interval asks accept ["interval_ends", mode] and ["interval_gap", n] to treat intervals separated by a small gap as conflicting/mergeable. count_pairs: for an int_list parameter (also give arg int_list, iterate on it, and at least one pair_test or pair_bound fact (at most one of each; if both are given a pair must satisfy both); no aggregate), counts pairs of POSITIONS (i, j) with i < j whose elements satisfy the test(s) (equal values at different positions form separate pairs); 0 for fewer than two elements. Example for 'pairs whose sum is divisible by 4': ["arg","numbers","int_list"], ["iterate","numbers"], ["ask","count_pairs"], ["pair_test","sum","4","0"]. Example for 'pairs whose sum is divisible by the parameter m': ["arg","m","int"], ["pair_test","sum","m","0"]. Example for 'pairs with |a-b| < k': ["pair_bound","abs_difference","lt","k"]. Example for inversions (i < j and list[i] > list[j]; equal values do not count): ["ask","count_pairs"], ["pair_bound","difference","gt","0"]. balanced_brackets: for a string parameter (give arg string, iterate on it, and at least one bracket_pair fact; no aggregate): scans the characters with a stack, every character that is not a declared bracket is ignored; the answer is True when every closing bracket matches the most recent unclosed opener of its own pair and nothing is left open (the empty string is balanced). Add ["bracket_output", form] for the maximum nesting depth or the position of the first error instead of the boolean. Example 'brackets ()[]{} balanced and properly nested': ["arg","s","string"], ["iterate","s"], ["ask","balanced_brackets"], ["bracket_pair","(",")"], ["bracket_pair","[","]"], ["bracket_pair","{","}"]. run_length: for a string parameter (or list; give arg, iterate on it; no aggregate): groups maximal runs of equal adjacent elements; by default the answer is the run-length-encoded string (each run written as the character followed by its length, add ["run_format","count_char"] to write length first, add ["run_one","omit"] to leave out a length of 1; the empty string gives ''). ["run_output", form] gives instead the list of [char, length] pairs, the number of runs, or the longest run length; ["run_output","decoded"] runs the encoding BACKWARDS: the string parameter is itself run-length encoded and the answer is the expanded string. Example 'compress a string, omitting counts of 1': ["arg","s","string"], ["iterate","s"], ["ask","run_length"], ["run_one","omit"]. Example 'decode a1b3 style text (character then digit count, count omitted for 1)': ["arg","s","string"], ["iterate","s"], ["ask","run_length"], ["run_output","decoded"]. diagonal_sums: for an int_matrix parameter (give arg int_matrix, iterate on it, exactly one diagonal_op fact, optional diagonal_center; no aggregate): sums the main diagonal cells (i, i) and the anti-diagonal cells (i, cols-1-i) and combines them as diagonal_op says. Example 'main diagonal sum minus anti-diagonal sum, centre cell counted only once (in the main diagonal)': ["arg","mat","int_matrix"], ["iterate","mat"], ["ask","diagonal_sums"], ["diagonal_op","difference"], ["diagonal_center","main_only"]. matrix_transform: for an int_matrix parameter (give arg int_matrix, iterate on it, exactly one matrix_op fact; no aggregate): the answer is a NEW matrix (list of lists) obtained by reorienting the input as matrix_op says. Example 'transpose of mat': ["arg","mat","int_matrix"], ["iterate","mat"], ["ask","matrix_transform"], ["matrix_op","transpose"]. simulate_ops: for an op_list parameter (give arg op_list, iterate on it; no aggregate): processes the operations in order on an initially empty container: ('push', x) adds x, ('pop',) removes and returns one element, ('peek',) returns one element without removing it. The container is a FIFO queue by default (pop/peek see the oldest element); add ["container","stack"] for LIFO (newest element). A pop/peek on an empty container returns the if_empty value (default None). By default the answer is the list of all values returned by pops and peeks in order; ["sim_output", form] gives instead the remaining contents, their number, or the number of pops/peeks on an empty container. Example 'FIFO queue, list of popped values, None for pop on empty': ["arg","ops","op_list"], ["iterate","ops"], ["ask","simulate_ops"]. best_pair: for an int_list parameter (give arg int_list, iterate on it, exactly one pair_value fact, optional result_floor / result_cap, and if_empty which is REQUIRED; no aggregate): over all pairs of positions i < j with a = list[i] (earlier) and b = list[j] (later) the answer is the largest or smallest value of the pair expression chosen by pair_value; if_empty is the answer when the list has fewer than two elements. result_floor n / result_cap n clamp a real pair result to at least / at most n. Example 'maximum profit buying at index i and selling at a later index j (price[j] - price[i]), 0 if no positive profit or fewer than two prices': ["arg","prices","int_list"], ["iterate","prices"], ["ask","best_pair"], ["pair_value","reverse_difference","max"], ["result_floor","0"], ["if_empty","0"]. Example 'largest drop from an earlier to a later element (earlier - later)': pair_value difference max. Example 'smallest sum of two elements, None if fewer than two': pair_value sum min with if_empty none. palindrome_check: for a string or int_list parameter (give arg, iterate on it; no aggregate/fold/select_rank/distinct): the iterated elements are filtered and mapped as usual (keep/drop/remainder/bound/map/floordiv/scale/add) and the resulting sequence is compared with its reverse. By default the answer is the boolean 'reads the same forwards and backwards' (True for an empty sequence). ["palindrome_tolerance", n] allows up to n mismatched mirrored pairs (almost-palindrome); ["palindrome_output", form] gives the number of mismatched mirrored pairs or the index of the first mismatch instead. Example 'palindrome ignoring non-alphanumeric characters and case': ["arg","s","string"], ["iterate","s"], ["ask","palindrome_check"], ["keep","alnum"], ["map","lower"]. Example 'palindrome after deleting at most one character' is NOT covered (tolerance counts mismatched pairs, not deletions). date_offset: calendar date arithmetic in the proleptic Gregorian calendar, for a date given as three int parameters (year, month, day; declare each with arg int, no iterate, no aggregate; also give date_fields naming them). By default the answer is the signed number of days from the date_origin date to the given date (positive when after, zero when equal, negative when before); ["date_output", form] gives instead the absolute number of days, the weekday (Monday = 0 .. Sunday = 6) or the day of the year (1-based). Example 'days from 2000-01-01 to the date y-m-d, negative before': ["arg","y","int"], ["arg","m","int"], ["arg","d","int"], ["ask","date_offset"], ["date_fields","y","m","d"], ["date_origin","2000","1","1"]. count_in_range: counts (or, with range_output sum, adds up) the integers x from range_from (default 1) to range_to (inclusive; an int parameter or a constant) that are selected by a divisibility rule list (range_rule facts, range_default); no iterate, no aggregate; constant time, so the bound may be huge. See range_rule for examples such as Gregorian leap years up to a year y. convert_case: for a string parameter (give arg string, iterate on it, case_to which is REQUIRED, optional case_from; no aggregate): rewrites the words of the string from the case_from naming style (default snake) into the case_to naming style and answers the new string ('' for the empty string). Example 'snake_case to lowerCamelCase': ["arg","s","string"], ["iterate","s"], ["ask","convert_case"], ["case_from","snake"], ["case_to","camel"]. shift_letters: for a string parameter (give arg string, iterate on it, shift_by REQUIRED, optional shift_set and shift_direction; no aggregate): a Caesar-style shift; every character of the chosen class is rotated by the shift amount within its alphabet (wrapping around) and all other characters are kept unchanged; the answer is the new string ('' for the empty string). Example 'shift every lowercase letter forward by n, n may be negative or larger than 26': ["arg","s","string"], ["arg","n","int"], ["iterate","s"], ["ask","shift_letters"], ["shift_by","n"]. eliminate_circle: Josephus-style circular elimination, no iterate, no aggregate; give circle_size (int parameter = number of people) and circle_step (every step-th person is removed); optional circle_output, circle_first, circle_start. Example 'n people numbered 1..n in a circle, count k and eliminate the k-th, continue from the next person, return the survivor': ["arg","n","int"], ["arg","k","int"], ["ask","eliminate_circle"], ["circle_size","n"], ["circle_step","k"]. digits_of_number: the decimal digits of a big number computed from an int parameter (no iterate, no aggregate): give number_of (which number: n!, the n-th Fibonacci number or base**n), optional digit_output (default the digit sum) and for power number_base. Example 'sum of the digits of n!': ["arg","n","int"], ["ask","digits_of_number"], ["number_of","factorial","n"], ["digit_output","sum"]. Example 'number of digits of 2**n': ["number_of","power","n"], ["number_base","2"], ["digit_output","count"].

number_of.doc: only for ask digits_of_number (exactly one, REQUIRED): which big non-negative integer is built from the int parameter n (declared with arg int, must be non-negative): factorial = n! (0! = 1), fibonacci = the n-th Fibonacci number (F0 = 0, F1 = 1), power = number_base ** n (default base 2; the digits of the absolute value are used).

number_base.doc: only for ask digits_of_number with number_of power (at most one, default 2): the base of base ** n, an integer constant or the name of an int parameter.

digit_output.doc: only for ask digits_of_number (at most one, default sum): sum = sum of the decimal digits, count = number of decimal digits (the value 0 has one digit), max_digit = largest decimal digit, trailing_zeros = number of zeros at the end of the decimal form (0 for the value 0; e.g. zeros at the end of n!).

shift_by.doc: only for ask shift_letters (exactly one, REQUIRED): the number of positions each shifted character moves forward (negative moves backward, any magnitude, taken modulo the alphabet size 26 for letters or 10 for digits). An integer constant or the name of an int parameter (declared with arg int). Example 'rot13': ["shift_by","13"]

shift_set.doc: only for ask shift_letters (at most one, default lower): which characters are shifted. lower = ASCII a-z (alphabet of 26), upper = ASCII A-Z, alpha = both a-z and A-Z (each case rotates inside its own alphabet), digit = 0-9 (rotates modulo 10). All other characters stay unchanged

shift_direction.doc: only for ask shift_letters (at most one, default forward): backward negates the shift amount, e.g. 'shift back by n' or decrypting a Caesar cipher

case_from.doc: only for ask convert_case (at most one, default snake): the naming style of the input string. snake = words separated by underscores (a_b_c), kebab = separated by hyphens (a-b-c), space = separated by single spaces, camel / pascal = words start at each uppercase letter (helloWorld / HelloWorld; every uppercase letter starts a new word). Empty words from repeated separators are ignored. Words are lowercased before being rewritten

case_to.doc: only for ask convert_case (exactly one, REQUIRED): the naming style of the answer. camel = lowerCamelCase (first word all lowercase, later words with first letter uppercased: hello_world -> helloWorld), pascal = UpperCamelCase (every word capitalised: HelloWorld), snake = lowercase words joined by '_', kebab = lowercase words joined by '-', constant = UPPERCASE words joined by '_' (HELLO_WORLD), space = lowercase words joined by single spaces, title = capitalised words joined by single spaces (Hello World)

date_fields.doc: only for ask date_offset (exactly one): the names of the three int parameters holding the year, month (1-12) and day of month of the date; the date is assumed valid and in the proleptic Gregorian calendar. Example: ["date_fields","y","m","d"]

date_origin.doc: only for ask date_offset (at most one): the constant reference date (year, month, day) that day counts are measured from. REQUIRED for the default output days and for abs_days (e.g. ["date_origin","2000","1","1"] or the Unix epoch ["date_origin","1970","1","1"]); ignored for weekday and day_of_year

date_output.doc: only for ask date_offset (at most one): days (default) = signed days from date_origin to the date; abs_days = absolute value of that; weekday = day of the week of the date, Monday = 0 .. Sunday = 6; day_of_year = 1-based position of the date within its year

pair_value.doc: only for ask best_pair (exactly one): the pair expression for positions i < j with a = list[i], b = list[j]: difference = a - b (earlier minus later), reverse_difference = b - a (later minus earlier, e.g. stock profit buy at i sell at j), sum = a + b, abs_difference = |a - b|. which selects the maximum or the minimum of that expression over all pairs. Runs in O(n) (O(n log n) for sum and abs_difference)

result_floor.doc: only for ask best_pair (at most one): a pair result below n is replaced by n, e.g. ["result_floor","0"] for 'return 0 if the best value is negative'. n is an integer constant or the name of an int parameter. Not applied to the if_empty answer

result_cap.doc: only for ask best_pair (at most one): a pair result above n is replaced by n. n is an integer constant or the name of an int parameter. Not applied to the if_empty answer

container.doc: only for ask simulate_ops (at most one, default queue): queue = FIFO (pop/peek take the oldest pushed element still present), stack = LIFO (pop/peek take the most recently pushed element still present)

sim_output.doc: only for ask simulate_ops (at most one): results (default) = list of the values returned by pop and peek operations in order (the if_empty value for those on an empty container); remaining = list of elements left in the container (oldest first for a queue, bottom first for a stack); size = how many elements are left; empty_count = number of pop/peek operations that found the container empty

matrix_op.doc: only for ask matrix_transform (exactly one): how the rows x cols matrix is reoriented. transpose = rows and columns swapped (out[j][i] = mat[i][j], result is cols x rows); rotate_cw = rotated 90 degrees clockwise (out[j][i] = mat[rows-1-i][j]); rotate_ccw = rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise (out[j][i] = mat[i][cols-1-j]); rotate_180 = rotated half a turn (both orders reversed); flip_horizontal = each row reversed (mirror left-right); flip_vertical = the order of the rows reversed (mirror top-bottom); anti_transpose = transpose along the anti-diagonal (out[j][i] = mat[rows-1-i][cols-1-j]). Input is not modified

diagonal_op.doc: only for ask diagonal_sums (exactly one): how the main-diagonal sum M and the anti-diagonal sum A are combined: difference = M - A, reverse_difference = A - M, sum = M + A, main = M only, anti = A only

diagonal_center.doc: only for ask diagonal_sums (at most one, default both): what happens to the centre cell, i.e. the cell lying on both diagonals (exists when the size is odd). both = it belongs to both diagonals (counted in M and in A); main_only = it is counted only in M (left out of A); anti_only = only in A; skip = left out of both. 'centre not counted twice' in a sum usually means main_only

min_depth.doc: only for ask covered_length (at most one, default 1): a point counts only when at least n valid intervals cover it (multiplicity counted: a repeated interval covers its points twice). n=2: 'covered by at least two'

max_depth.doc: only for ask covered_length (at most one, default unbounded): a point counts only when at most n valid intervals cover it. With min_depth equal to n it means 'covered by exactly n'; max_depth 1 with default min_depth = covered exactly once

pair_test.doc: only for ask count_pairs (at most one): a pair of positions i < j with elements a = list[i], b = list[j] qualifies when (a op b) % m == r using Python's % (non-negative remainder for positive m); m must be non-zero. m is an integer constant or the name of an int parameter (declared with arg int, e.g. the runtime modulus m); r is an integer constant. op: sum = a + b, difference = a - b, abs_difference = abs(a - b), product = a * b. 'Divisible by m' is r = 0. Examples: ["pair_test","sum","4","0"] = sum divisible by 4; ["pair_test","sum","m","0"] = sum divisible by parameter m; ["pair_test","difference","3","0"] = congruent mod 3; ["pair_test","sum","2","1"] = odd sum; ["pair_test","product","2","0"] = even product

pair_bound.doc: only for ask count_pairs (at most one; may be combined with pair_test, both must hold): a pair of positions i < j with elements a = list[i], b = list[j] qualifies when (a op b) cmp n, with op as in pair_test and cmp: lt <, le <=, gt >, ge >=, eq ==, ne !=. n is an integer constant or the name of an int parameter (declared with arg int), compared directly with no modulus. If the threshold makes the comparison impossible (e.g. abs_difference < k with k <= 0) the count is naturally 0. Examples: ["pair_bound","abs_difference","lt","k"] = |a-b| < k; ["pair_bound","sum","ge","10"] = a+b >= 10; ["pair_bound","abs_difference","le","k"] = |a-b| <= k; ["pair_bound","difference","gt","0"] = a > b (inversions)

pair_output.doc: only for ask count_pairs or overlap_pairs: form of the answer. count (default): number of qualifying pairs. exists: boolean, is there at least one qualifying pair. all: boolean, do all pairs qualify (True when there are fewer than two elements). At most one

pair_relation.doc: only for ask overlap_pairs (at most one, default overlap): which pairs of valid intervals qualify. overlap = the two intervals share a point (respecting interval_ends and interval_gap); disjoint = they do not

interval_output.doc: only for ask merge_intervals: form of the answer computed from the merged intervals. intervals (default): the merged [start, end] list. merged_count: number of merged intervals (closed: [1,2],[3,4] stay separate, only [1,2],[2,3] merge; half-open: [1,3],[3,5] stay separate). covered_count: closed = number of distinct integers covered (end - start + 1 each); half-open = total covered length (end - start each). gap_count: uncovered integers (closed) / uncovered length (half-open) strictly between the smallest start and the largest end (0 when at most one merged interval). longest_covered: length of the longest merged interval (end - start + 1 closed, end - start half-open). Numeric forms answer 0 for an empty list. At most one. Example: ["interval_output", "covered_count"]

interval_ends.doc: only for interval asks (max_overlap, merge_intervals, overlap_pairs, covered_length): end-point convention of the interval_list pairs. half_open (DEFAULT) = [start, end): end excluded, [1,3],[3,5] do not overlap and are not merged, start >= end is empty and ignored, merged output is again half-open. closed = [start, end]: both ends included, touching intervals such as [1,3],[3,5] conflict/merge, start == end is a valid single point, start > end is invalid and ignored. State ["interval_ends", "closed"] whenever the statement says closed/inclusive. At most one

interval_gap.doc: only for interval asks (max_overlap, merge_intervals, overlap_pairs, covered_length) (at most one, n >= 0, default 0): gap tolerance. Each interval's end is treated as n units later when deciding conflicts/merges, i.e. a later interval starting at b1 conflicts with / merges into an earlier one ending at a2 when b1 <= a2 + n (closed) or b1 < a2 + n (half_open). Validity of intervals is unchanged. Example: closed bookings where [1,3] and [4,6] conflict because no free integer lies between them: ["interval_ends","closed"] plus ["interval_gap","1"]; 'at least 2 free days between bookings' would be gap 0 conflicts only if start <= end + 2 -> ["interval_gap","2"]. With merge_intervals, intervals within the gap are merged and the merged end is the larger original end

at_least.doc: only for ask max_overlap: the answer becomes the boolean (maximum overlap >= n) instead of the integer maximum. n=2: some two non-empty intervals overlap; n=3: some point is covered by at least three intervals. At most one. Example: ["at_least", "2"]

start.doc: shortest_path start: ["corner", "top_left"|"bottom_right"] or ["char", <the start character, e.g. "S">]. Default corner top_left

goal.doc: shortest_path goal: ["corner", "top_left"|"bottom_right"] or ["char", <the goal character, e.g. "E">]. Default corner bottom_right

unreachable.doc: answer when the goal cannot be reached / target cannot be formed. Default -1

items.doc: knapsack-style: the list of item values (coins, step sizes, numbers); values must be positive, zeros are allowed only with use once. The items come from a list parameter; for a FIXED constant item set written in the statement use items_literal instead. In a staged problem the list may be the output of an earlier stage, written stage1, stage2, ...

items_literal.doc: knapsack-style alternative to items for a CONSTANT item set that is not a parameter (e.g. a frog taking 1, 2 or 3 steps, coins 1, 5, 10). The single argument is a Python list literal of integers written as one string, e.g. ["items_literal", "[1, 2, 3]"]. Use instead of items (never both); everything else (target, ask, use, order, unique, modulo, terms, unreachable) works as for items. The target may be an int parameter (arg int, target n); a negative target then yields no solution (0 / False / unreachable answer). Example 'ordered sequences of jumps of 1, 2 or 3 summing to n' (n = 0 gives 1, negative gives 0): ["arg","n","int"], ["items_literal","[1, 2, 3]"], ["target","n"], ["ask","count_ways"], ["order","matters"]

items_range.doc: knapsack-style alternative to items / items_literal for a CONSECUTIVE range of item values lo..hi inclusive (e.g. jumps of 1 to k steps with k an int parameter). lo and hi are integer constants or names of int parameters (declare them with arg int); lo must be at least 1; hi < lo means no items. Never combine with items / items_literal. Supported asks: count_ways with ["order","matters"] (ordered sequences of parts from lo..hi summing to the target, unlimited use; target 0 gives 1, negative target gives 0), min_count (fewest parts, unreachable answer otherwise, default -1) and feasible. modulo (count_ways), unreachable and a target that is an int parameter work as for items. use once, unique and terms are NOT supported with items_range (use items / items_literal then). Example 'ordered jumps of 1..k steps summing to n, modulo 1000000007': ["arg","n","int"], ["arg","k","int"], ["items_range","1","k"], ["target","n"], ["ask","count_ways"], ["order","matters"], ["modulo","1000000007"]

unique.doc: knapsack-style: repeated values in this items list are ignored, only distinct values count as choices. Give it the same param as the items fact. Example: ["unique", "step_sizes"]

target.doc: the integer total to be formed exactly. In a staged problem it may be the (int) output of an earlier stage, written stage1, ...

use.doc: each item may be used unlimited times, or at most once (each list position once). Default unlimited

order.doc: for count_ways: are different orderings of the same multiset counted separately? Default ignored

modulo.doc: answer is reported modulo this number

terms.doc: knapsack-style (with items, target, ask count_ways/feasible/min_count): bounds the NUMBER of items used by the int parameter `param` (declare it with arg int). exactly: the total uses exactly that many terms (0 terms form only total 0); at_most: at most that many terms. Works with order matters/ignored, use unlimited/once (not once+matters), unique, modulo (count_ways only). A negative bound or negative target gives no solution (0 / False / unreachable answer). count_ways sums over the allowed term counts; feasible = some allowed count works; min_count = fewest terms among allowed counts. Example: ["terms", "exactly", "k"] with ["order", "matters"], ["ask", "count_ways"] counts ordered sequences of exactly k terms summing to the target

bracket_pair.doc: only for ask balanced_brackets (one fact per bracket kind, at least one): the single character that opens a bracket and the single character that closes it, e.g. ["bracket_pair","(",")"], ["bracket_pair","<",">"]. Use only one pair for 'parentheses only' problems; all other characters are ignored. A character may take part in only one pair and must differ between open and close

bracket_output.doc: only for ask balanced_brackets (at most one): form of the answer. balanced (default): boolean, properly nested and fully closed. max_depth: the maximum nesting depth reached (0 when there are no brackets), or -1 when the brackets are not balanced. error_index: -1 when balanced; otherwise the 0-based index of the first closing bracket that does not match the innermost open bracket (or has none), and if no such closer exists the index of the most recent unclosed opening bracket

run_format.doc: only for ask run_length with the default encoded output or with run_output decoded (at most one): char_count (default) writes each run as the character then its length ('a3b2'); count_char writes the length first ('3a2b'). With decoded it states which layout the input string uses (a missing count means 1; run characters must not be digits)

run_one.doc: only for ask run_length with the encoded output (at most one): omit leaves out the length when a run has length 1 ('a2bc5'); keep (default) always writes it ('a2b1c5'). Not needed for decoded: decoding accepts both

run_output.doc: only for ask run_length (at most one): encoded (default) = the run-length-encoded string; pairs = list of [element, length] per maximal run in order; run_count = number of maximal runs (0 for empty input); longest_run = length of the longest run (0 for empty input); decoded = the input string is itself run-length encoded (character followed by its decimal count, or count first with run_format count_char; a missing count means 1) and the answer is the expanded string ('' for the empty string)

palindrome_output.doc: only for ask palindrome_check (at most one): check (default) = boolean, the filtered/mapped sequence has at most palindrome_tolerance (default 0) mismatched mirrored pairs; mismatch_count = number of mirrored pairs (i, n-1-i) with i < n-1-i whose elements differ; first_mismatch = smallest such index i, or -1 when the sequence is a palindrome

palindrome_tolerance.doc: only for ask palindrome_check with the default check output (at most one, default 0): up to n mismatched mirrored pairs are allowed. n is an integer constant or the name of an int parameter (declared with arg int)

range_to.doc: only for ask count_in_range (exactly one): the inclusive upper end of the integer range being scanned: an integer constant or the name of an int parameter (declared with arg int), e.g. the year y in 'leap years from 1 through y'. An empty range (upper end below the lower end) gives 0

range_from.doc: only for ask count_in_range (at most one, default 1): the inclusive lower end of the integer range: an integer constant or the name of an int parameter (declared with arg int). Use it for 'between years a and b'

range_rule.doc: only for ask count_in_range (any number of facts): one divisibility rule. Each integer x of the range gets the verdict of the rule with the SMALLEST rank whose divisor d divides x (x % d == 0), or range_default when no rule matches. d is a non-zero integer constant or the name of an int parameter (declared with arg int); verdict yes = x is selected, no = x is not selected; ranks are distinct integers that only fix the order of testing. Example 'Gregorian leap years from 1 through y' (divisible by 4 except centuries not divisible by 400): ["arg","y","int"], ["ask","count_in_range"], ["range_to","y"], ["range_rule","1","400","yes"], ["range_rule","2","100","no"], ["range_rule","3","4","yes"], ["range_default","no"]. Example 'integers 1..n divisible by 3 or 5': rules 3 yes and 5 yes, default no. Example 'integers 1..n NOT divisible by k': one rule k no with range_default yes. Example 'sum of the multiples of m up to n': one rule m yes, default no, range_output sum

range_default.doc: only for ask count_in_range (at most one, default no): the verdict of an integer matched by no range_rule; yes = selected, no = not selected

range_output.doc: only for ask count_in_range (at most one, default count): count = how many selected integers, sum = the sum of the selected integers

circle_size.doc: only for ask eliminate_circle (exactly one, REQUIRED): the name of the int parameter (declared with arg int) holding the number of people standing in the circle. People are numbered circle_first .. circle_first + n - 1 in circle order.

circle_step.doc: only for ask eliminate_circle (exactly one, REQUIRED): every amount-th person is eliminated, counting the person where counting starts as 1; an integer constant or the name of an int parameter (declared with arg int); must be positive and may be much larger than the circle. After an elimination counting restarts with the next person. Example 'count k people and eliminate the k-th': ["circle_step","k"]; 'every second person': ["circle_step","2"]

circle_output.doc: only for ask eliminate_circle (at most one, default survivor): survivor = the number of the last remaining person; order = the list of all people in the order they are eliminated (the survivor comes last)

circle_first.doc: only for ask eliminate_circle (at most one, default 1): the number given to the first person of the circle; use 0 for people numbered 0..n-1 (0-indexed variant)

circle_start.doc: only for ask eliminate_circle (at most one, default = circle_first): the number of the person where counting begins (that person is counted as 1); an integer constant or the name of an int parameter

size.doc: only when the statement states a bound: list/string length, grid cells, or an integer parameter's magnitude. tiny <= 1e2, small <= 1e3, medium <= 1e5, large <= 1e6, huge <= 1e7, vast beyond. Without a stated bound the generator assumes medium for the main sequence, small for item lists, and the magnitude seen in the tests for integers

guarantees.doc: a property the statement explicitly guarantees for a parameter (e.g. 'a list of positive integers' -> positive; 'distinct denominations' -> distinct). Omit what the statement does not say: algorithms with preconditions are refused when the guarantee is missing

source.doc: where the elements of a stage (any sequence-input schema: seq_fold, seq_rank, seq_reduce, palindrome_check, run_encode, pair_count, pair_extreme, bracket_match, interval_scan) come from (iterate(A) is the short form of source param A). source range LO HI = the integers LO..HI inclusive (each an integer literal, an int parameter or, in a staged problem, the int output of an earlier stage written stage1 ...); source digits X = the decimal digits (ints) of the integer X; source chars X = the characters of the string X; X is a parameter or, in a staged problem, the output of an earlier stage written stage1, stage2, ...; source stage I = the elements of the list (or characters of the string) output by stage I. Give y only for range (the upper bound).

stage.doc: STAGED PROBLEM: the answer is computed by a chain of stages; stage I is declared with stage I <schema> (any of the listed schemas: seq_fold, seq_rank, seq_reduce, palindrome_check, run_encode, pair_count, pair_extreme, bracket_match, interval_scan, knapsack), consecutive from 1, and the last stage gives the answer. The schema is the one the stage's own facts derive (e.g. a stage with select_rank is seq_rank, one with ask count_pairs is pair_count, one with items + target + ask count_ways is knapsack). The facts that describe stage I are written with the stage index glued to the predicate name, e.g. ["1.source","range","1","n"], ["1.aggregate","product"], ["2.source","digits","stage1"], ["2.aggregate","sum"] (every vocabulary predicate of the stage's schema may be used this way: source, keep, drop, remainder, bound, map, aggregate, cond, expr, filter, select_rank, ask, pair_test, items, target, ...). Parameters are described by ordinary arg facts. A stage may read parameters and the outputs of earlier stages only: its sequence through a source (or iterate), a knapsack stage its items and target as ["2.items","stage1"] / ["2.target","t"], a range bound as ["2.source","range","1","stage1"]. A stage output can only feed an input of the same type (list of ints -> a sequence source or items, an int -> digits, a range bound or target, a string -> chars or a string sequence). Single-stage problems do not use stage at all.

cond.doc: a leaf of a condition tree on the element x (used with expr and filter): cond ID keep C / cond ID drop C (C as in keep/drop), cond ID remainder M R (x % M == R), cond ID bound OP N (OP as in bound). Ids are free names; each id is defined once.

expr.doc: an inner node of a condition tree: expr E and X Y / expr E or X Y (X, Y are cond or expr ids) / expr E not X (one operand). No cycles. Example, leap years: cond d4 remainder 4 0; cond d100 remainder 100 0; cond d400 remainder 400 0; expr n100 not d100; expr a and d4 n100; expr e or a d400; filter e.

filter.doc: the root of the condition tree: only elements for which the tree holds take part (and-ed with any keep/drop/remainder/bound facts). All cond/expr nodes must be reachable from it.
